text.p: Mary T. Meagher start looking over your shoulder because American Misty Hyman and Australian Susan O'Neill are taking aim at your 16-year-old 100 and 200 metre butterfly world records.

While both admit their goals are incredibly difficult -- in the swimming world Meagher's marks are considered harder to break than Bob Beamon's legendary long jump mark which lasted 23 years -- they said they were enjoying the chase.
Hyman's next shot at the 100, the mark she is closest to, comes on Tuesday, the third day of the Pan Pacific Swimming Championships.
"It's an honour to know that I'm even close to such a record," Hyman said. "I'm enjoying the pursuit."
Hyman won the 100 at U.S. national championships late last month in 58:72 seconds, the quickest time over the distance in three years, and the sixth quickest ever.

Meagher, the great U.S. swimmer of the early 1980s, set the world record for the 100 butterfly at the U.S. nationals on August 16, 1981, with a time of 57.83 seconds, three days after setting the record in the 200 with a time of 2:05.96.

Hyman at 18, may appear to have a better shot at the 100 mark than the 24-year-old O'Neill has at the 200, but time may not be on her side as well. Hyman uses a unique start and underwater fish kick to stay underwater for up to 30 metres at the start, and usually emerges with a strong lead over her opponents.

"She might be fighting the clock as some people believe FINA (international swimming's ruling body) may change the rules to outlaw those starts after the world championships," said head U.S. women's coach John Collins.

The world championships are in Perth in January. O'Neill won the 200 easily on Sunday in Fukuoka but her winning time of two minutes 8.59 seconds -- while the best this year -- was still well back of Meagher's record of 2:05.96.

"I know the 200 is the one I'm looking at," O'Neill said, who won the event with a timing of 2:07.29 at the Atlanta Olympics. "It's a pretty big goal and I'm not sure I can get it before my career is over. Obviously, Mary T is a pretty big legend."
O'Neill has become one of Australia's most popular women athletes, along with golfer Karrie Webb and track star Cathy Freeman.
Meagher now lives in Atlanta, where she has a child and is married to Mike Plant, the president of the Goodwill Games, said Charles Snyder, a spokesman for the U.S. swimming federation.

"You would need an extraordinary amount of talent to break those records," said Collins, who watched Meagher set her marks. About 300 swimmers from 22 countries and regions are competing in the Pan Pacific meet, a major run-up event to the world championships.
